title: White v. Corlies & Tifft
summary: An offer made to a party at a distance is accepted only by an outward act placed in a proper course of communication so that it will ordinarily reach the offeror; a builder’s private decision to accept, followed by buying and working lumber equally suited to other jobs, communicated nothing and was mere preparation, so the merchants could still countermand.
notes: Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1871).

sections.Parties: White, a builder with a business on Fortieth Street in New York City, was the plaintiff and respondent on appeal. Corlies and Tifft, merchants doing business on Dey Street who wanted a suite of offices at 57 Broadway fitted up, were the defendants and appellants. Judge Folger wrote for the Court of Appeals of New York on November 20, 1871; the casebook spells the name Tift.
sections.Material Facts: In September 1865 the merchants gave White specifications for fitting up the offices and asked for an estimate, which he delivered on September 28; they changed the specifications that day and he assented to the changes, but no agreement was complete. They had first wanted black walnut within twenty-one days, which White said he could not do, then asked for an estimate in white pine; his estimate named no completion time. On September 29 their bookkeeper sent White a note saying that upon an agreement to finish the fitting up of the offices within two weeks from that date he could begin at once. White did not reply. He at once bought lumber and began working on it at his own shop; the lumber and the work suited other comparable jobs. The next day the merchants countermanded the proposal and asked for another estimate in black walnut.
sections.Procedural History: White sued for damages, contending that his conduct had accepted the proposal before the countermand. The trial judge instructed the jury that White need not have gone back to the merchants and said he had begun, and that he could act on the note and commence the job; the defendants excepted. The jury found for White, and the General Term of the First Judicial District affirmed. The Court of Appeals reversed and ordered a new trial, with costs to abide the event; Justice Allen did not vote.
sections.Issue: Did White accept the merchants’ September 29 proposal by privately deciding to proceed and by buying and working on materials suitable for any comparable job, without any act that communicated assent to the merchants or set such a communication in motion?
sections.Holding: No. The note was a proposal requiring acceptance, and an offer made when the parties are apart must be accepted by an appropriate outward act. The act need not have reached the offeror’s knowledge before a contract forms, but it must be put in a proper course of communication so that it will ordinarily reach the offeror within a reasonable time. White’s private intention, and his purchase of lumber usable on other jobs, gave the merchants no indication of assent and did not set one in motion; they were preparation, not acceptance. The instruction was erroneous and a new trial was ordered.
sections.Reasoning: The court found no earlier contract in the evidence and treated the bookkeeper’s note as a proposal requiring acceptance. Where parties are apart, assent must be shown by an outward act: a mailed acceptance illustrates the distinction, because dispatch may complete the contract before delivery when the offeree has taken an objectively communicative step. White’s conduct failed that test. The lumber he bought and the work he did on it suited other jobs of the kind, so his acts did not identify this undertaking as the one accepted; his private intention explained them to himself but gave the merchants no outward sign. The court did not hold that conduct can never accept an offer or that actual receipt of notice is always required, only that general preparations coupled with an uncommunicated intention were insufficient under this proposal. Under the later Restatement the case would be analysed by asking whether the offer invited a promise or performance and by separating preparation from the beginning of invited performance under §§ 45 and 62, with §§ 54 and 56 addressing notice.

priorVersions.summary: Private preparation using materials suitable for other jobs did not put an acceptance into a reasonable course of communication.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Court of Appeals of New York (1871).

Compare Ever-Tite’s express invitation to commence performance. The excerpt supports an inquiry into the offer and the communicative significance of conduct, not a universal rule that preparatory activity can never have legal significance.

sections.Parties: White, a builder, sued Corlies & Tifft, merchants seeking work on their offices.
sections.Material Facts: The parties exchanged specifications and an estimate. The merchants’ note stated that, upon an agreement to finish within two weeks, White could begin at once. White made no reply. He bought lumber and began working on it privately. The materials and work were suitable for other jobs. The merchants countermanded the next day.
sections.Procedural History: A jury found for White under an instruction that beginning the work sufficed. The Court of Appeals of New York reversed and ordered a new trial because that instruction did not require an appropriate manifestation of acceptance.
sections.Issue: Did White’s uncommunicated conduct accept the merchants’ proposal?
sections.Holding: No acceptance was shown by the conduct described. A mental decision, accompanied only by ambiguous private preparation, did not bind the offeror.
sections.Reasoning: Acceptance must be manifested through an appropriate act, at least placed in a proper course for reaching the offeror in a reasonable time. Actual knowledge at the instant of formation is not always necessary: the opinion itself uses mailing an acceptance as an example. White’s conduct neither indicated this particular agreement nor set an indication in motion. The editors explore alternative readings of the estimate and the words “upon an agreement,” rather than assuming those phrases have only one possible meaning.

learning.why: White helps separate preparation, acceptance by conduct, and notification. The categories depend on what the offer invites and what the offeree actually communicates.

topics.acceptance: A private decision and ambiguous preparations did not manifest acceptance.
topics.assent: Conduct must communicate agreement in its context.
topics.notice-acceptance: The court distinguishes putting notice in motion from actual receipt.
topics.performance-acceptance: The offer’s wording and the specificity of the work determine whether conduct counts.

mnemonic.rationale: Lumber bought before the offer was accepted
